s05.slug: SUNDAY · 4:20 PM · DUPRE STREET — THE HOUSE THAT CAN’T SIT DOWN
body: By twenty past four the sun has got down into the oaks at the end of Dupre Street, and it comes in the front windows low and yellow and lies across the rug, the couch, and the big television, where Channel 4 has had the pre-game on since two. On the screen it is still bright afternoon in Miami. Seventy-some thousand people are finding their seats in the sun. In the house on Dupre Street the couch is empty and the room is full.

body.text: Remy gets them home four hours after King Arthur, by way of a short cut through Uptown that he still believes in and a cousin’s porch on Napoleon Avenue where he stopped for one beer. He comes up the steps first with the twins and a pillowcase of throws over his shoulder, and Jack comes up behind him with Laney’s purple beads still round his neck. It went on without him: Lena’s roux in Mémère’s big pot on the back burner, the lid cocked, and Mémère’s spoon laid across it.
body.else: Jack has been in this house since the roux. The gumbo on the back burner is the one he cut the onions for, five hours on, down to dark in Mémère’s big pot with the lid cocked, and he has been sent from it twice since, once for andouille and once to the attic for the folding chairs. The parade came home at one with Remy and a pillowcase of throws. Laney fell asleep sitting up on the porch swing with a stuffed football in her lap, and Theo spent an hour explaining the Colts’ secondary to Tony, who let him.

body: Since four the house has been filling. People come up the steep steps without knocking and in through the screen door with their hands full: the lady from across the street with a king cake in a bakery box, purple and green and gold sugar coming off it onto the cellophane; a couple from the corner with a foil pan of jambalaya; and a big slow man in a Saints visor from two doors down who brings his own cooler of Abita, his own folding chair, and a boombox, which he sets on the porch rail and turns up. People stand in the front room with a bowl in one hand and a spoon in the other and their eyes on Miami, and when one of them shifts to let somebody by, everybody shifts, a slow tide of elbows going round the furniture.

On the porch rail the boombox is all piano and horns and a voice going up and up about Carnival when Nonc Clovis comes up the steps. Jack knows him for a Broussard from the bottom step: Tony’s face with less of it, shorter and quicker and brown as a saddle, in a gold Saints windbreaker, with a folding chair under one arm and a leash in the other hand. At the end of the leash, taking the steps one at a time and stopping on each to reconsider, is a basset hound in a black-and-gold bandana.
“*Nonc!*” Josie yells, and the twins come out from under the dining table at a run.

At the top of the steps Clovis finds the tune and comes in with the boombox, loud, every word of the first verse right, conducting the porch with the leash hand. At the end of the verse he stops singing as if somebody had pulled his plug, and the song goes on into the chorus without him, and he lets it, and comes in.

“Nonc knows the first verse of everything,” Remy says, going past Jack with a beer. “Only the first. Him and Daddy and them put this house back after the water, and Nonc sang the first verse of every song on the radio for two years straight. Mama about killed him.”
Clovis sets up his chair inside the door and looks Jack over. “This the Ohio boy?”
“Yes, sir.”

“Browns.” Clovis shakes his head over it. He holds out the leash, and Jack, not knowing what else to do with it, takes it. “That’s Aints III. I named the first one in 1980. Bag year.” He sits. The dog sits on Jack’s foot. “The first one was ashamed. This one’s made his peace.”

Lena comes through from the kitchen with a stack of Mémère’s heavy bowls against her hip and her free arm going round her uncle’s neck on the way past. Her hair is up with the pencil through it again.

body.text: “Youngstown cut the onions,” she tells Clovis, over the bowls. Clovis looks at Jack, and through the kitchen door at the pot, and back. “Small?” “Small enough,” Lena says. “Mémère only had to tell him twice.”

He has had it in his inside pocket since King Arthur, with his hand over it most of the way home. He takes it out now and holds it out to her: the medallion bead, a gold crown stamped on the disk. Lena looks at it. She puts the bowls down on the arm of the couch and takes it from him and puts it over her head, and it comes down on top of the Miraculous Medal, the crown over the Virgin, and she picks up the bowls again and carries them on into the kitchen, and not one word.

body: In the kitchen Celeste puts an empty Igloo into his arms on her way past the stove. “Ice, baby,” she whispers. “The freezer in the shed.” He gives the leash to Josie and goes down the back steps with it, and comes back up them with it full and heavy against his chest. Celeste points him up the hall with her knife: the porch, for the man in the visor.

Luc is at the counter when he comes in with it. He is in uniform, the dark blue shirt with the patch and the badge, the belt with everything on it, a radio on his shoulder muttering numbers to itself, and he is eating a bowl of gumbo standing up, fast and neat, with his back to the window. “All hands in the Quarter tonight,” Tony says, coming through with a dish towel. “Every badge in the city.” Luc doesn’t add to it. He rinses his bowl and puts it in the drainer, and kisses his mother on the side of the head at the stove, and comes up the hall behind Jack and the ice. In the front room he bends down in front of Mémère’s armchair, a long way down, and she puts her thumb on his forehead and makes a small cross there, and says something in French for him only.
On his way out he stops in front of Jack, who is stuck in the crush by the door with the cooler in his arms. Luc looks at him. It isn’t long.
“Take care of the house.”

And he is out the screen door and down the steps. The room goes on eating. When Jack turns around, Lena is at the far end of the hall in the kitchen doorway with the ladle held up out of the pot, and a drop of gumbo is running down the handle onto the inside of her wrist. Her eyes go from the screen door to him. She puts her wrist to her mouth and turns back to the stove.
Remy climbs up on the coffee table and says, “*Seats.*”

body.title: Masking tape along the bottom of the television, in purple marker
body.text:
VIKINGS SEATS. DO NOT MOVE.
MAMA — COUCH (CORNER) · REMY — ARM · TESS + LUCILLE — FLOOR BY TV · NONC — HIS CHAIR BY THE DOOR · MÉMÈRE — HER CHAIR · JOSIE + JUDE — UNDER THE TABLE · DADDY — PORCH
NO NEW SEATS. NO TRADES.

body: “I wrote it down,” Josie says from under the dining table, “so there’s no arguing.”

Since the NFC Championship, Tess explains from the floor by the television, with Lucille asleep on her chest in the black-and-gold cap, every Broussard watches from wherever they sat when Hartley’s kick went through, and they have not lost since. Theo gets up off the arm of the couch without being told. Celeste takes her corner, Remy his arm. Clovis and the twins and Mémère are already where the tape says.
Margot reads the tape. “So the seating chart is load-bearing.”
“Everything in this house is load-bearing,” Remy says. “Daddy built it.”
“*Me*, I built the stairs,” says Clovis.

Tony comes up the hall with a kitchen chair hooked over his forearm and his radio in the other hand, a battered silver transistor with a coat hanger for an antenna. He stops in front of the television long enough for Miami to go by on his face.
“I was on the porch for the overtime,” he tells the room. “I’m on the porch.”

He goes out. Through the screen Jack watches him lean over the boombox on the rail. “Sorry, Ferd. I need the rail.” He unplugs it in the middle of the chorus, and the transistor goes up in its place, and the WWL men come on, low and fast and serious, and Ferd moves his folding chair over beside Tony’s kitchen chair, and the two of them sit with their backs to the window and listen to a pre-game they could watch by turning their heads.

Mémère takes the guests in hand. She puts her slipper to the footstool and slides it across the rug to Margot — “You.” — and Margot sits on it with her knees up under her chin. A dining chair has appeared at Mémère’s elbow, and Mémère pats it, and Kevin, her rosary partner since eleven, sits down in it and takes back the beads she hands him. Celeste whispers Theo and Laney down to the far end of the couch, and they go, and sit very close together and very straight and take a deep interest in the coin-toss graphics.

Which leaves Jack, and Lena, come out of the kitchen with a bowl of gumbo in each hand. He spent that Sunday in January at a taco truck. She spent it on a table at Sully’s with a bell rope in both hands. There is no seat in this house for either of them.
“We weren’t here for the Vikings,” Lena tells her grandmother.
Mémère looks at them over her beads.
“Those two,” she says. “On the floor. In front. Where I can see them.”
Lena hands him one of the bowls. She sits down cross-legged on the rug in front of the couch, with her back against it below her mother’s knees, and settles her bowl in her lap.
“She means it as a punishment,” she says.

She doesn’t move over. She has sat down in the middle of the rug, and the middle is where he sits. His knee is against hers. Her shoulder is against his arm. Aints III comes round the coffee table and lies down across both their feet with a groan from somewhere deep in the bandana. The gumbo is dark and smoky and hotter than it looks, and the heat of it comes up slow, after you’ve decided it isn’t coming. A piece of her hair has come loose from the pencil and lies along the side of her neck, down to the collar of her shirt, where the chain of the medal goes under it. He eats his gumbo.

He has had three spoonfuls when the RAZR goes off against his hip. On the outside screen, a long 330 number he has never saved and would know in his sleep. He hands Lena his bowl and gets up off the floor, and Lena watches him go, through the kitchen and out the back door and down onto the steps.

He opens it. The same flat woman. “This is a prepaid call from —” and into the gap, fast, his brother’s own voice: “Danny.” “— an inmate at Trumbull Correctional Institution. This call is subject to monitoring and recording. To accept, press one.”
He presses one.
“Professor.”
“Dan.”

Behind Danny, the dayroom: a television up high and loud, the same pre-game, half a second ahead of the one in the front room, and a room of men talking over it. “Gina says you’re at the Saints girl’s house for the Super Bowl and you’re calling it a road trip.”
“I didn’t call it anything.”
“That’s what I mean.”

Jack sits down on the back steps. The yard is in shadow already, the big boil pot washed out and turned upside down on the picnic table, and over the roof of the shed the sky is going the clear deep blue it goes before it gives up.
“Where are you right now?” Danny says.
“Back steps. Her old man’s out front on the porch with a radio. He won’t watch.”
“He won’t watch the *Super Bowl*.”
“He couldn’t watch the overtime against the Vikings. He went out on the porch with the radio, and they won. So now he’s on the porch.”
Danny laughs, low. “That’s a smart man. That man knows how it works.” The dayroom yells at something. “Who you got?”
“Who do you think.”
“Me too. The room’s got Indianapolis except me and Reggie, and Reggie’s got whoever I got.” Somebody behind him wants the volume up and gets it. “Ma lit a candle for the kicker again.”
“Hartley.”
“She don’t know his name. She lit it for *the kicker*. Side altar at St. Brigid’s, a dollar in the box. Gina says Father Dom watched her do it and pretended he didn’t see.”

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners. The Friday before I flew back she took the phone for ten seconds to ask was I eating. When I come to New Orleans I come to her house first. Thursday at seven in the morning she called me herself, from Dupre Street, on a number the redhead gave her. She knew I’d said yes. She called anyway: I don’t come because the rich boy asked me, I come because she asked me. Don’t bring nothing. Come to this house first — I said it back to her. Lena told her not to call. Saturday night on the porch she cancelled Theo’s hotel. You sleep here. Boys in the attic. She sleeps in the front room, where she can see the stairs. Sunday she was dressed for the eight o’clock before seven, in her chair with the lamp on. One of you is up; the other two sleep like Protestants. For the game she put Lena and me on the floor, in front, where she could see us.

journal.title: Clovis Broussard
journal.text: Tony’s younger brother; one of the brothers who put the house back. Knows the first verse of everything, and only the first. His dog is Aints III, in a Saints bandana. The first one was ashamed. This one’s made his peace.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas, his twenty-third, he called from Trumbull and got Skye. Gina’s envelope hadn’t come — two cards in it, she says, and one with a candle. Skye’s letter came, in capitals. Ma wouldn’t tell him the name of the song. Skye told him how I tricked her — a long caper, a love spell in Gloria’s crust — and he laughed till they told him to keep it down. Family news, he said. Then she told him what really happened in Montecito, and he coughed for a while. She asked him to call again. I told him she’s the one I can tell the truth to. He said I’m not subtle. He’s still going with the trick. Super Bowl Sunday he called collect from the dayroom before the kickoff. I’m at the Saints girl’s house for the Super Bowl and I’m calling it a road trip. Ma lit a candle for the kicker again. Watch the game, he said. All of it.

choices.text: “I wish you were here for this.”
response: “Me too,” Danny says. “I’d be out on the porch with the old man. I like him already.” Somebody near the phone wants to know is he gonna be all day. “Watch the game, Professor. All of it.”

The woman cuts in. “You have one minute remaining.” They spend it on nothing much: the dayroom chili, the cold in Leavittsburg, and Reggie’s opinion of Peyton Manning, which Danny declines to repeat on a recorded line.
When Jack comes back in and sits down on the rug, his bowl is waiting on the floor in his place with the spoon standing up in it. Lena looks at him once, and back at Miami, and doesn’t ask.

“I’ll tell her. She’ll light another one.” Danny’s voice has a grin in it. “She’s gonna have that side altar lit up like Christmas by the fourth quarter. Father Dom’s gonna have to call the fire department.”
“You have one minute remaining,” says the woman.
“Watch the game, Professor,” Danny says. “All of it.”

Back in the front room Aints III has taken his half of the rug and is asleep on it. Lena puts her hand on the dog’s backside and shoves, and the dog gets up and lies down again on the far side of her, sighing, and Jack sits where it was, warm. She gives him back his bowl. She looks at him once, and then at the screen.
A silence on the line the length of a dayroom.
“Watch the game, Professor. All of it.”

The line clicks, and it’s the yard again, and a horn somewhere toward Esplanade blowing the Who Dat over and over. Inside, he sits down on the rug where he was, and Lena hands him back his bowl, still warm; she has had it on her own knee. She looks at him once and goes back to the television.
